contributions.headingText: Cardiac haemangiomas are a family of benign vascular tumours arising in the heart and are broadly divided morphologically as capillary, cavernous, and arteriovenous types.

9120/0 Haemangioma, NOS

9122/0 Venous haemangioma

9131/0 Capillary haemangioma

9123/0 Arteriovenous haemangioma

9121/0 Cavernous haemangioma

2F01 & XH3U29 Benign neoplasm of intrathoracic organs & Capillary haemangioma

2F01 & XH1GU2 Benign neoplasm of intrathoracic organs & Cavernous haemangioma

2F01 & XH5AW4 Benign neoplasm of intrathoracic organs & Haemangioma, NOS
Not recommended: cardiac angioma; cardiac vascular malformation.

Haemangiomas may arise from the endocardium, myocardium, or pericardium. The ventricular free walls are the most common sites of involvement. Congenital haemangiomas most frequently involve the right atrium {22529610; 15549621; 19340361}.

Most cardiac haemangiomas are asymptomatic and incidental. Symptomatic patients may present with dyspnoea, palpitations, murmur, or (unusually) thromboembolic events. Arrhythmia and conduction disturbances may be related to an intramyocardial location. Pericardial involvement may lead to effusion, haemopericardium, or potentially tamponade {30935649; 28803417}. Congenital haemangiomas, frequently associated with pericardial effusion, may be diagnosed in utero {1947327; 26929881; 28803417}. The malformation type of cardiac haemangioma has been rarely reported with in Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome {17845155}.

Age at presentation ranges widely, from the neonatal period to old age. Approximately 10% of cases occur in children, and 10% are diagnosed in utero or in infancy {22529610}. There is a slight male predominance.
The clinical evolution and clinicopathological features suggest that these lesions represent vascular malformations.
Tumours are usually single and nodular. Intramyocardial lesions often merge with the adjacent tissue, whereas endoluminal lesions (80% of the cases) can be sessile or polypoid {2129569; 17420812}.

The histological patterns, which overlap, are capillary, cavernous, and arteriovenous. The most frequent type is cavernous, followed by mixed cavernous-capillary and capillary. Cardiac haemangiomas with adipocytes similar to intramuscular haemangiomas are very rare. Atrial haemangiomas may be diagnostically challenging because of the trabeculations of the atrial wall.

Capillary haemangiomas consist of small, thin-walled vessels arising from and clustered around a larger “feeder” vessel. Small capillary lumina may be difficult to immediately appreciate in cellular lesions. The intervening stroma may have a myxoid character, and scattered pericytes and fibroblasts may be seen. So-called infantile haemangiomas, which are considered a type of capillary haemangioma, contain back-to-back capillaries and no intervening fibrous tissue {15549621}. In this later type, mitoses may be numerous at the proliferative stage and immunohistochemical expression of GLUT1 is characteristic {15549621}.

Cavernous types exhibit large, dilated vascular spaces, often situated within the myocardium itself. The vessels may be thin- or thick-walled, and pools of blood may be present throughout.

The arteriovenous types are characterized by arterial and venous structures, the latter of which often exhibit remodelling and arterialization owing to complex arterial anastomoses and exposure to systemic pressures. Similar to in the extracardiac variety, adipose tissue and collagen may be admixed.

Essential:

  • Benign tumour composed of thin-walled vascular spaces, without atypia

Desirable:

  • Expression of CD31, CD34, and ERG
Surgical excision of haemangioma is generally successful, with rare postsurgical events {2129569}.
